history.q: Which ancient Arab people carved the city of Petra into rose-red cliffs?
history.fact: The Nabataeans grew rich controlling incense and spice caravans, and carved Petra's tombs straight into the sandstone.

history.q: Which empire annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106 CE?
history.fact: Emperor Trajan turned the kingdom into the province of Arabia Petraea, and a new road, the Via Traiana Nova, soon ran to the Red Sea.

history.q: In which year did Transjordan gain independence from Britain?
history.fact: Independence came on 25 May 1946, still celebrated as Independence Day; Emir Abdullah was proclaimed king the same day.

history.q: Which country administered Transjordan under a League of Nations mandate after the First World War?
history.fact: The British Mandate covered Palestine and Transjordan, but from 1921 Transjordan was run as a separate emirate under Abdullah.

history.q: Which royal dynasty has ruled Jordan since the founding of the emirate in 1921?
history.fact: The Hashemites trace their descent to the Prophet Muhammad through his great-grandfather Hashim, from whom the family takes its name.

history.q: Which British officer, known as 'Lawrence of Arabia', fought alongside Arab forces in the Arab Revolt of 1916-1918?
history.fact: A rock formation in Wadi Rum is nicknamed the Seven Pillars of Wisdom after Lawrence's memoir, and the 1962 film was partly shot there.

history.q: Which king ruled Jordan from 1952 until his death in 1999?
history.fact: Hussein was proclaimed king at just 16 after his father Talal abdicated, and reigned for more than 46 years.

history.q: The Roman-era city of Gerasa is known today by what name?
history.fact: Jerash is one of the best-preserved Roman provincial towns anywhere, with an oval plaza ringed by Ionic columns.

history.q: Which empire controlled the lands of modern Jordan for about four centuries until the First World War?
history.fact: The Ottomans took the region in 1516-17 and held it for roughly 400 years, until the Arab Revolt and British forces pushed them out in 1918.

history.q: The Mesha Stele, found at Dhiban in 1868, was set up by a king of which ancient kingdom?
history.fact: Carved around 840 BCE, the stele was broken soon after its discovery and pieced back together; it now stands in the Louvre.

history.q: What was Amman called in the Greco-Roman era?
history.fact: The name honoured Egypt's Ptolemy II Philadelphus; the city's Roman Theatre, seating about 6,000, still sits in downtown Amman.

history.q: In 636 CE, Arab Muslim armies decisively defeated the Byzantines at a battle named after which river?
history.fact: The Yarmouk, which today forms part of Jordan's northern border, gave its name to a battle that ended Byzantine rule over Syria.

history.q: Who became the first emir of Transjordan in 1921?
history.fact: A son of Sharif Hussein of Mecca, Abdullah ruled as emir for 25 years before becoming Jordan's first king in 1946.

history.q: Which Swiss explorer, travelling as 'Sheikh Ibrahim', became the first European in centuries to describe Petra, in 1812?
history.fact: Burckhardt said he wished to sacrifice a goat at Aaron's tomb so that his guide would lead him through the hidden city.

history.q: Which leader launched the Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire in June 1916?
history.fact: Sharif Hussein, Emir of Mecca, was King Abdullah II's great-great-grandfather; Jordan's flag echoes the revolt's banner.

history.q: Amman's name comes from which Iron Age people, whose capital stood on the city's citadel hill?
history.fact: Their capital, Rabbath Ammon, stood on Jabal al-Qal'a, where the Amman Citadel now shows Roman, Byzantine and Umayyad ruins.

history.q: Gerasa (Jerash), Gadara (Umm Qais) and Philadelphia (Amman) belonged to which group of Greco-Roman cities?
history.fact: 'Decapolis' means 'ten cities'; most lay in today's Jordan and Syria, with Scythopolis just west of the Jordan River.

history.q: Ajloun Castle in northern Jordan was built in the 1180s by a commander serving which leader?
history.fact: Built by Saladin's general Izz al-Din Usama, the hilltop fort watched over the Jordan Valley and routes contested with the Crusaders.

history.q: Which crusader lord, notorious for raiding Muslim caravans, held Kerak Castle in the 1180s?
history.fact: Saladin personally executed Raynald after the Battle of Hattin in 1187, and Kerak itself surrendered to Saladin's forces in 1188.

history.q: Which British officer, nicknamed 'Abu Hunaik', commanded Jordan's Arab Legion until King Hussein dismissed him in 1956?
history.fact: 'Glubb Pasha' led the Legion from 1939; his dismissal marked the Arabisation of the army's command.

history.q: The Neolithic site of 'Ain Ghazal, on the edge of Amman, is famous for which discovery?
history.fact: Made around 9,000 years ago, the statues are among the oldest large-scale human figures ever found; some are shown at the Jordan Museum.

history.q: Bozrah, the ancient capital at today's Buseira in southern Jordan, belonged to which Iron Age kingdom?
history.fact: Edom lay south of the Dead Sea; the Hebrew Bible links its people to Esau, and its land later became Nabataean territory.

history.q: Under which king, who reigned from about 9 BCE to 40 CE, did Nabataean Petra reach its greatest splendour?
history.fact: Aretas IV called himself 'lover of his people'; many of Petra's grandest monuments, possibly including the Treasury, date from his reign.

history.q: In 1878 the Ottomans settled which refugee people among the ruins of Amman, reviving it as a village?
history.fact: Circassians from the Caucasus refounded Amman; their descendants still provide a ceremonial guard at the Royal Court.

history.q: The Battle of Mu'tah in 629, near Karak, pitted early Muslim forces against which empire?
history.fact: After three Muslim commanders fell, Khalid ibn al-Walid led the army's withdrawal and, by tradition, earned the title 'Sword of God'.

technology.q: How did the Nabataeans sustain a large city in Petra's arid valley?
choices: By channelling rainwater into rock-cut cisterns
By pumping groundwater with steam engines
By importing ice from the mountains
technology.fact: Petra's engineers built dams, terracotta pipes and cisterns to capture flash floods, enough to feed fountains and even a garden pool.

technology.q: Which mineral, harvested from vast Dead Sea evaporation ponds, makes Jordan one of the world's leading exporters?
technology.fact: Potash is a key fertiliser ingredient; the Arab Potash Company has produced it on the Dead Sea's southern shore since the 1980s.

technology.q: Which Ottoman railway through Jordan did T. E. Lawrence and Arab forces repeatedly sabotage?
technology.fact: Opened to Medina in 1908, the line ran from Damascus via Amman and Ma'an to carry pilgrims, and troops, south to the holy cities.

technology.q: How did Nabataean masons carve Petra's great façades, such as the Treasury?
choices: From the bottom up, on scaffolding
technology.fact: Masons cut a ledge at the cliff top and worked downward, so the finished upper sections never needed scaffolding.

technology.q: Petra's tombs and temples are carved directly into what kind of rock?
technology.fact: Iron and other minerals streak Petra's sandstone in pinks, reds and yellows, earning it the nickname 'Rose City'.

technology.q: Why do swimmers float so effortlessly in the Dead Sea?
choices: It is fed by hot springs
Its water is extremely salty and dense
technology.fact: The Dead Sea is roughly 34% salt, nearly ten times saltier than the ocean, so its dense water pushes bathers up like corks.

technology.q: What is the name of Jordan's national airline, founded in 1963?
technology.fact: Its hub, Queen Alia International Airport, is named after King Hussein's third wife, who died in a helicopter crash in 1977.

technology.q: Which aromatic tree resin, carried by caravans through Petra, helped make the Nabataeans rich?
technology.fact: Frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia were burned in temples across the Roman world, and Nabataean routes carried them north.

technology.q: The Tafila project in southern Jordan, opened in 2015, was the kingdom's first large farm of which energy source?
technology.fact: Tafila's 38 turbines sit on windy highlands above the Dead Sea rift and generate about 117 megawatts.

technology.q: Jordan is a major exporter of which rock, mined at Eshidiya and Al-Hasa to make fertilisers?
technology.fact: Phosphate has been mined in Jordan since the 1930s, and much of it is shipped out through the Red Sea port of Aqaba.

technology.q: Which logistics company, founded in Amman in 1982, became the first Arab-based company listed on NASDAQ?
technology.fact: Aramex was co-founded by Jordanian entrepreneur Fadi Ghandour and listed on NASDAQ in 1997; it is now headquartered in Dubai.

technology.q: Which Arabic web portal and email service, founded in Jordan in 2000, was bought by Yahoo! in 2009?
technology.fact: Maktoob, meaning 'written' in Arabic, was co-founded by Samih Toukan and Hussam Khoury and was a pioneer of Arabic webmail.

technology.q: Which canal, begun in 1959, carries irrigation water along the east side of the Jordan Valley?
technology.fact: Originally called the East Ghor Canal, it draws on the Yarmouk River and turned the valley floor into Jordan's winter vegetable garden.

technology.q: Since 2013, a pipeline of about 325 km has carried ancient groundwater to Amman from which aquifer?
technology.fact: The Disi aquifer, shared with Saudi Arabia, holds 'fossil' water that fell as rain thousands of years ago and is barely replenished.

technology.q: Jordan holds some of the world's largest deposits of which fuel resource, now burned at the Attarat power plant?
technology.fact: Oil shale is rock rich in kerogen; the Attarat plant, south-east of Amman, is one of the largest power stations built to burn it directly.

technology.q: Jordan's first satellite, the JY1-SAT CubeSat launched in 2018, was named after the radio call sign of which king?
technology.fact: King Hussein was a keen amateur radio operator who chatted with enthusiasts around the world under the call sign JY1.

technology.q: To protect Petra's Siq from flash floods, how did Nabataean engineers divert the Wadi Musa stream?
choices: With a dam and a rock-cut tunnel
Into the Dead Sea via a canal
technology.fact: Their dam sent floodwater through a tunnel around the gorge; after a deadly flood in 1963 a modern dam was built on the same spot.

technology.q: SESAME, opened near Allan in Jordan in 2017, was the Middle East's first what?
technology.fact: Built under UNESCO's auspices, SESAME's members include Cyprus, Egypt, Iran, Israel, Jordan, Pakistan, Turkey and the Palestinian Authority.

technology.q: Wadi Faynan in southern Jordan was one of the ancient world's great centres for producing which metal?
technology.fact: Huge slag heaps at Khirbat en-Nahas reveal large-scale copper smelting in the Iron Age, and the Romans later worked mines here too.

technology.q: The Umayyad bathhouse of Qusayr Amra has a dome painted with what pioneering image?
choices: A map of the heavens with zodiac figures
technology.fact: Its 8th-century dome is one of the earliest surviving depictions of the night sky on a hemispherical surface.

technology.q: Which ancient city in northern Jordan was supplied by the longest known tunnel of antiquity, explored only in the 2000s?
technology.fact: The Gadara Aqueduct's main tunnelled section runs for roughly 94 km, winding along the hills' contours like an underground canal.

technology.q: Nabataean potters were famed for what kind of fine tableware?
technology.fact: Thrown on fast wheels, the bowls had walls only a couple of millimetres thick and were painted with delicate leaves and palmettes.

technology.q: Jordan's first nuclear reactor, a research reactor inaugurated in 2016, stands at which university?
choices: Jordan University of Science and Technology
technology.fact: The 5-megawatt Jordan Research and Training Reactor near Irbid produces medical isotopes and trains the kingdom's nuclear scientists.

technology.q: Which prince founded Jordan's Royal Scientific Society in 1970?
technology.fact: Prince El Hassan, King Hussein's younger brother, was crown prince for 34 years and has long championed science and dialogue.

technology.q: Which German engineer directed construction of the Hejaz Railway?
technology.fact: 'Meissner Pasha' built the line largely with Ottoman soldiers as labour; work began in 1900 and the railhead reached Medina in 1908.
